x.ASV: A Song of Ascents; of David. If it had not been Jehovah who was on our side, Let Israel now say,
x.Darby: A Song of degrees. Of David. If it had not been Jehovah who was for us — oh let Israel say —
x.KJV: A Song of degrees of David. If it had not been the Lord who was on our side, now may Israel say;
x.YLT: A Song of the Ascents, by David. Save for Jehovah--who hath been for us, (Pray, let Israel say),

nt: David is making a conditional statement **If not Yahweh**, that sounds hypothetical, but he knows that the condition is not true. Yahweh was indeed for Israel, and therefore the disastrous results David goes on to describe did not happen. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that the speaker believes is not true. Alternate translation: [If Yahweh had not been on our side]

David is saying what he wants the people of Israel to do and inviting them to join in communal recitation. See the discussion in the introduction to Psalms about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [Israel should indeed say]

x.ASV: If it had not been Jehovah who was on our side, When men rose up against us;
x.Darby: If it had not been Jehovah who was for us, when men rose up against us,
x.KJV: If it had not been the Lord who was on our side, when men rose up against us:
x.YLT: Save for Jehovah--who hath been for us, In the rising up of man against us,

nt: Here David is speaking as if the enemies attacking the Israelites actually **rose up** physically above Israel to destroy them. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. [when our enemies came to fight against us]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **man**. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [people]

x.ASV: Then they had swallowed us up alive, When their wrath was kindled against us:
x.Darby: Then they had swallowed us up alive, when their anger was kindled against us;
x.KJV: Then they had swallowed us up quick, when their wrath was kindled against us:
x.YLT: Then alive they had swallowed us up, In the burning of their anger against us,

nt: Here and through verse 5, the word **then** introduces what the consequences could have been if the condition proposed in the previous verse (if Yahweh had not been with them when their enemies attacked) had actually happened. Use a natural form in your language for introducing the consequence of this possible condition. Alternate translation: [in that case,]

Here David is speaking as if the enemies who could have killed all the Israelites were wild animals that could have **swallowed** Israel **alive**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [then they would have killed us all]

The pronoun **they** refers to the enemies described as “man” in verse 2. The singular “man” has shifted to a plural pronoun here and following. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [then those enemies]

David is using **nose burned** as a common expression of his culture to mean “to be very angry.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they were fiercely angry with us]

x.ASV: Then the waters had overwhelmed us, The stream had gone over our soul;
x.Darby: Then the waters had overwhelmed us, a torrent had gone over our soul;
x.KJV: Then the waters had overwhelmed us, the stream had gone over our soul:
x.YLT: Then the waters had overflowed us, The stream passed over our soul,

nt: Here David is speaking of the attacks of the enemies as if they were **waters** and a **torrent** that was like a river overflowing its banks or a flood that could overwhelm and drown Israel. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Then the enemies would have overwhelmed us; the attacks would have destroyed us]
Here, **soul** represents the people themselves. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [all of us]

x.ASV: Then the proud waters had gone over our soul.
x.Darby: Then the proud waters had gone over our soul.
x.KJV: Then the proud waters had gone over our soul.
x.YLT: Then passed over our soul had the proud waters.

nt: This phrase is basically repeating the two phrases from the previous verse; “the waters would have overflowed us” and “the torrent would have passed over our soul,” The second and third phrases emphasize the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could begin this phrase with a connecting word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [Then indeed, our enemies would have completely annihilated us]
Here, **soul** represents the people themselves. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [all of us]

x.ASV: Blessed be Jehovah, Who hath not given us as a prey to their teeth.
x.Darby: Blessed be Jehovah, who gave us not up a prey to their teeth!
x.KJV: Blessed be the Lord, who hath not given us as a prey to their teeth.
x.YLT: Blessed is Jehovah who hath not given us, A prey to their teeth.

nt: The expression **Blessed be** is a passive verbal form. The psalmist is expressing his desire to praise Yahweh. If it would be unnatural to use that form for this purpose, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [We bless Yahweh] or [Let us praise Yahweh]

Here David is speaking of the enemies attacking and destroying Israel as if they were predatory animals that could devour Israel as **prey** with **their teeth**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [who did not hand us over to be destroyed by our enemies]

The pronoun **their** refers to the enemies described as “man” in verse 2 and “they” in verse 3. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [for the teeth of our enemies]

x.ASV: Our soul is escaped as a bird out of the snare of the fowlers: The snare is broken, and we are escaped.
x.Darby: Our soul is escaped as a bird out of the snare of the fowlers: the snare is broken, and we have escaped.
x.KJV: Our soul is escaped as a bird out of the snare of the fowlers: the snare is broken, and we are escaped.
x.YLT: Our soul as a bird hath escaped from a snare of fowlers, The snare was broken, and we have escaped.

nt: The point of this comparison is that just as a **bird** that **escaped from the snare of the trappers** flew away to safety, so the people of Israel escaped from the power of their enemies. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [We are like a bird that escaped from the trap of the hunters]

David is using the term **soul** to mean the entire person from the perspective of his spiritual and emotional existence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [We are like a bird]

The expression **was broken** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the snare broke]

David is stating the pronoun **we** separately, even though the verb translated as **we escaped** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize the tension of the escape. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing this emphasis. Alternate translation: [and we indeed escaped!]

x.ASV: Our help is in the name of Jehovah, Who made heaven and earth.
x.Darby: Our help is in the name of Jehovah, the maker of heavens and earth.
x.KJV: Our help is in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth.
x.YLT: Our help is in the name of Jehovah, Maker of the heavens and earth!

nt: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **help**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [It is Yahweh himself who helps us]

David is using the term **name** to represent who Yahweh is and his authority and power. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [is in Yahweh himself]

David is referring to all of creation by naming two extremes, **heaven** and **earth**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [of all things]
